stories.headline: As the 'Peanut Punch' takes over NFL, how do teams counter it?
stories.summary: After Charles Tillman popularized the punch 14 years ago, it has really taken off this season.
stories.body:
ORCHARD PARK, N.Y. -- On Oct. 11, New York Giants running back Cam Skattebo fumbled away a win. The Giants lined up in field goal range coming out of the two-minute warning in overtime. Any points would have won the game.

Washington Commanders defensive lineman Daron Payne had other thoughts. After Skattebo was hit in the backfield and had to use his forearms to shed a tackle, he couldn't get the ball back up to his chest. Payne threw his blocker out of the way and threw his fist at the daylight between Skattebo and the football. Ball out. The Giants' chance at a win was erased, and the game ended in a tie.

Payne executed an increasingly popular -- and violent -- maneuver called the "Peanut Punch," wherein a would-be tackler throws a haymaker at the football in an attempt to pop it loose rather than wrapping up the ball carrier -- a technique popularized around 2012 and named after former Chicago Bears defender Charles "Peanut" Tillman.

One day later, Buffalo Bills running back James Cook III fell victim to the same fate.

Carrying from the Los Angeles Rams' 22-yard line early in overtime, Cook squeezed the ball low, around the left side of his abdomen. Had Cook had the ball higher, the incoming punch from linebacker Nate Landman might have left a bruise, but the ball wouldn't have had anywhere to go.

With the ball at Cook's side, Landman found a crease between Cook's armpit and wrist and wedged the ball through. Ball out. Rams possession. Had it not been for a blocked field goal minutes later, Cook's fumble would've meant Bills defeat.

But with fumbles come consequences.

Though the Giants didn't explicitly call it a benching, Skattebo didn't receive any carries the week following his fumble. And despite Cook being the NFL's reigning rushing leader, Bills coach Joe Brady threatened punishments -- including decreased playing time if Cook didn't clean up his ball security.

The NFL does not track punch attempts or their success as official statistics, and punches are almost impossible to track given the way defenders wield their arms while going for tackles, but it's clear that some of the NFL's best and most reliable ball carriers struggle with it.

Since the start of the 2025 season, including the playoffs, Cook has fumbled 11 times to lead all running backs, a rate of once for every 44 carries. Skattebo, while not as prolific in total rushes, fumbles once every 40 carries.

Defenders are punching at the ball nearly every drive, and being labeled a ball security risk makes you a target. The more you fumble, the more opponents try to make you fumble. As Brady puts it, every team the Bills play will have on the scouting report to punch at Cook.

So as Cook and the fumble-prone Bills (6-1) prepare for their matchup against the Minnesota Vikings (6-1), who led the NFL in forced fumbles in 2025, let's examine the Peanut Punch's popularity, why it works, what offenses can do to counteract its effectiveness and what the state of ball security is in this ever-changing league.

Countering the Peanut Punch
Offenses know how to prevent the punch. The technique exists.

Carry the ball "high and tight," squeezing it across your chest diagonally at an incline.
One point of the ball should be in the crook of your elbow.
The other point needs to be somewhere between your chin and your opposite shoulder.
Apply pressure with your fingertips, bicep, forearm and rib cage.
Lower your pads.
Make sure your wrist is always above your elbow.
Make sure there's no air between the ball and your body.
Make sure the ball isn't visible from behind.
And when you sense contact coming, think "double in trouble" and brace by crossing your off-ball hand over your on-ball wrist.

The technique works, but ball security is a lot like darts. Darts isn't difficult because no one's cracked the mystery of how to throw a bulls-eye. It's tricky because there's a huge gap between knowing what to do and being able to do it with precise consistency every time.

The punch has been more successful because carrying a football properly defies basic human instinct. We don't pick up speed by tucking our arms into our ribs. We don't change direction with our wrists above our elbows. And we don't fall to the ground without using our hands.

As long as ball carriers are human, there's always going to be a sliver of daylight for defenders to punch at.

"You've got to realize you've got the baby in your hands," former All-Pro running back Jamal Lewis told ESPN. "You've got the game in your hands. You've got the play in your hands when you're carrying the football. It's really just understanding that this is not a natural running style."

'High and tight'

Lewis fumbled 22 times in his first three full seasons. He wasn't alone. Over the same four-year span (Lewis missed the 2001 season with a knee injury), Giants stalwart Tiki Barber fumbled 35 times.

Reflecting on that period, Barber told ESPN he didn't think he had a ball security problem. A newspaper reporter actually tipped Barber off to just how frequently he'd been putting the ball on the ground, and it wasn't until 2004 when coach Tom Coughlin arrived in New York when Barber started to foresee consequences.

"Coughlin comes in and he says 'Tiki, you're a great player, but if you keep fumbling you're not going to play,'" Barber said.

So Barber and running backs coach Jerald Ingram went into the lab. "High and tight" became Barber's entire life. Anywhere he went, he had a football high and tight. On the treadmill. In the meeting room. Walking to the cafeteria.

He instructed teammates to try to rake the ball away from him any time, anywhere.

"It ultimately became second nature, so when I got in the games I wasn't even thinking about it anymore," Barber said. "You know what's interesting is I've been retired for 20 seasons now, but whenever somebody throws me a football, the first thing I do is put high and tight. It's so ingrained in my mind, I can't not do it."

After fumbling once every 27 carries from 2000 to 2003, Barber fumbled just once every 112 carries from 2004 to 2006, making the Pro Bowl all three years and twice leading the league in scrimmage yards.

Lewis noticed. Sometime after his 2,000-yard season in 2003 with the Baltimore Ravens, Lewis says he saw a TV special about Barber's adherence to the high-and-tight lifestyle and adopted it as his own. After fumbling once every 46 carries from 2000 to 2003, Lewis only fumbled once per 90 carries for the rest of his career.

All these years later, Lewis is still such a believer in the importance of high and tight that he scours the internet for proof of its efficacy. Lewis says he was watching footage of current Ravens running back Derrick Henry's workouts before the 2025 season and felt Henry was pumping the ball too much when he ran. Henry fumbled in each of that season's first three games.

This year, Lewis says he saw more of a high-and-tight ball security emphasis in Henry's offseason workout footage. Through nine weeks, Henry fumbled once only in 175 carries.

Punch specialists

The Bears drafted Tillman in 2003, but his patented punch didn't become well-known until 14 years ago this week when Tillman forced four fumbles in the same game. What's standard practice today barely existed during Barber's and Lewis' heydays.

Today's ball carriers have to contend with punch specialists on just about every defense. In Baltimore, there's Marlon Humphrey. In Atlanta, there's safety Jessie Bates III, who seems to jar a ball loose every weekend. In San Francisco, there's All-Pro linebacker Fred Warner, who led the league with four forced fumbles through the season's first seven games and is even more renowned for forcing fumbles in practice.

"I think obviously they all understand what it requires to protect the ball anytime they're practicing against me," Warner said, "which in turn is obviously going to make it easier on game day when they're out there having to try to protect the ball."

Aware of this truth, teams like the Bills put scout team defenders in jersey numbers belonging to players like Humphrey, Bates and Warner and instruct those players to punch more liberally than normal to simulate in-game conditions.

Defensive coaches crave the punch too. Falcons defensive coordinator Jeff Ulbrich remembers a time when he was on staff with the New York Jets when Tillman came out to conduct a Peanut Punch presentation.

Bates says the emphasis on the punch has grown significantly over his nine-year career. It's been incorporated into early-practice turnover drills, just as much a hallmark of training as tip drills and deflection drills. And it's not a one-size-fits-all exercise. Bates says there are different punching techniques depending on whether you're behind the ball carrier (called an ambush) versus if the runner has the ball in transition.

Titans cornerbacks coach Tony Oden, who was also on those Jets staffs, is so Zen about coaching the punch that he teaches players to punch with their eyes, not their fists.

"You punch it with your eyes because to see something, you have to look at it," Oden continued. "It can't be a blind punch. You punch with your eyes, your hand's going to follow. You try to punch the air behind the ball. A lot of times you think about just punching the ball.

"The ball's a big surface. Punch the middle of the ball, you don't hurt your wrist and those kind of things. You punch the air behind the ball [adjacent to the ribs] because that's the sweet spot."

Bills running backs coach Kelly Skipper says the Peanut Punch is "all you see" on film these days. Bills back Ty Johnson says he gets punched every time he carries the ball, so much so he barely notices anymore.

San Francisco linebacker Dre Greenlaw was recently fined $12,537 for an errant Peanut Punch attempt that clocked Falcons receiver Drake London in the helmet. In response to the incident, Greenlaw bluntly says: "I ain't punching no more."

But even if the ball isn't coming out and on occasion a missed punch could mean a penalty, fine or touchdown, defenses are confident the body blows add up.

"They have to make a decision in traffic," Oden said. "Sometimes it slows them up a little bit in regards to fighting for extra yards. If they know you have a potential or mindset of attacking the ball, when they protect it a little bit, the feet stop, they don't get as many leaky yards."

Leveling the playing field

Per ESPN Research, there were more fumbles per carry among running backs through the first eight weeks of this season than any since 2016. But that stat might overplay the Peanut Punch's effectiveness.

In 2025, NFL teams fumbled 536 times. That's by far the fewest number of total fumbles in any season since the AFL-NFL merger (1970). The only other season with fewer than 600 fumbles was 2020 (597). The rate of team fumbles per game has decreased steadily every decade in the Super Bowl era, with 2025 being the first time that teams fumbled less than once per game.

Discounting QB fumbles, in 1975 there was one fumble for every 21 run plays. By 2005, it was one fumble per 33 run plays. In 2025, that rate cratered to one fumble for every 51 rush attempts.

"If I had played in this era where guys are punching at it, I wouldn't worry about it," Barber says. "I worried more about these massive linemen and linebackers who would be stripping the ball away from me. They'd grab my hand basically breaking my wrist and then it's like 'I can't hold onto the ball because you're just stronger than me.'"

Cook led all non-quarterbacks with six fumbles last season. In 1975, there were 23 non-quarterbacks who fumbled six or more times -- with teams playing 14 games per season back then.

The Jets' Braelon Allen had been one of the NFL's best running backs since taking over for an injured Breece Hall in Week 4. In the five-game absence, he had the second most rush yards behind Tampa Bay's Bucky Irving, but even he was caught by the punch Sunday. Kansas City Chiefs linebacker Nick Bolton was able to jar the ball loose, causing Allen to lose his first fumble of the season, and only second since being drafted in 2024.

"Since I've been in the league to where I am now, every year it's more and more emphasis on getting the ball out," Titans running back Tony Pollard said, pointing at the paradox of the numbers. "It feels like making the tackle is secondary to punching it out. You can notice that a lot. A lot of guys, they rather get the ball out than secure the tackle."

The sacrifice of running with the ball high and tight is that it can make it harder to cut. Quick lateral movement is almost impossible without moving your arms. But Barber says tighter arm swings also lead to choppier steps which made him feel faster, and lower pad level made him run more powerfully.

Defenders have to make trade-offs too. While it's most common for the punching defender to be a pursuit player trailing a play, it's becoming more common for defenders to go for a punch before the runner has been wrapped up. That leads to arm tackles and opportunities for ball carriers to win with power.

Consider a fourth-and-1 play the Bills ran in Week 8 versus Baltimore. Cook received a pitch on a speed option. Ravens safety Malaki Starks wrapped Cook up with one arm behind the line to gain. Linebacker Roquan Smith came flying in, fist out, to finish the play. Cook saw Smith coming, squeezed the ball high and tight under his chin and slapped his off-ball hand over his wrist for protection.

Smith's punch connected wrist to ball. The ball barely moved. Cook kept churning his legs and stretched through the would-be tacklers for a first down. Textbook. From double-in-trouble to safe with a new set of downs.

Again, there's no mystery to beating the punch. It's just a pain in the hand, wrist, forearm, chest and sometimes neck to deal with.

To a running back, that's just part of the job.

"The next play," Barber concludes, "is always more important."

NFL Nation reporters Ben Baby, Nick Wagoner, Turron Davenport and Marc Raimondi contributed to this report.

stories.headline: Lando Norris praises McLaren for win, celebrates mastering São Paulo conditions
stories.summary: Lando Norris hailed one of his best wins after conquering the weather in São Paulo a week after losing his status as world champion.
stories.body:
Lando Norris hailed one of his best wins after conquering the weather in São Paulo a week after losing his status as world champion.

The British driver claimed his third win in a tricky season, passing Kimi Antonelli when the new title holder spun out from the lead in cold and slippery conditions.

Norris never looked back and crossed the line 14.6 seconds clear of Max Verstappen, who completed another stunning comeback drive from the back of the Interlagos grid.

The 26-year-old's only mishap of the day came as he celebrated his win with his trademark slamming down of the champagne bottle on the podium, only for it to shatter in his hands.

But Norris was toasting his victory after the race, saying: "It's up there [with my best] in terms of challenge to achieve. Not been easy for all reasons possible.

"Conditions, weather, important to not make mistakes. A lot thrown at everyone on a day like today, but probably our best race in terms of execution.

"I forced Kimi to push, he went into a mistake I could capitalize on. From my side not making any mistakes which is so easy to do. Great performance from the team."

Pole-sitter Norris lost the lead to Antonelli off the line in damp conditions before also dropping a place to Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson at Turn Two.

"I probably can't say [how I felt] or I will get a fine!" Norris added.

"I wasn't too pleased, but I knew things could easily change and a lot could happen."

- Lando Norris holds off Max Verstappen to win São Paulo Grand Prix

- Mercedes completes the double with constructors' title at São Paulo Grand Prix

- Lando Norris takes third win this season in upgraded McLaren - as it happened

Verstappen started 21st, a place behind Lewis Hamilton after engine penalties for the pair. Hamilton soared to ninth after lap one, while the Dutchman soon ignited and was charging through the field.

He won this race from 17th in 2024 and was showing similar brilliance in the wet again, roaring past Hamilton as he closed in on the leading pack.

Norris reclaimed the lead having closed by pitting for soft tires a lap earlier, with Antonelli complaining of "something weird" with his car before he spun at Turn One.

He was off again as Verstappen progressed and Isack Hadjar also cruised through on his way to finishing third.

Antonelli allowed teammate George Russell through to come home fifth, with both Mercedes struggling with tyres on the day they clinched the constructors' title.

"I am very disappointed for the race, very angry to be fair, but I put that to the side for now because we clinched the title for the team. I am very happy for them," Antonelli said.

"Disappointing because we were on for the win, once I got temperature I had rhythm. I don't know why I lost the rears so quickly. We lost the race there."

Russell's hopes of a podium were undone when he spun on the exit of the narrow pit lane after his first stop, dropping him down to eighth.

Norris remains sixth in the championship but closed to within five points of fifth-placed Charles Leclerc as he moved towards the scrap for second, with Verstappen now 17 points clear of third-placed Russell.

The McLaren driver is pleased with the team's progress as they look towards 2027 but knows there is more to come.

"It is about good strategy, good pit stops, but I had a car I could fight for a win with today," Norris added.

"As much as we are happy, we are not as happy as we could be but we know we are not at the level we need to be yet. We are getting there slowly but we have work to do."

stories.headline: Thunder get Nique Clifford in trade with Kings
stories.summary: The Thunder have acquired 2025 first-round pick Nique Clifford in a trade with the Kings.
stories.body:
The Kings have traded second-year wing Nique Clifford to the Thunder for two second-round picks, Oklahoma City announced Sunday.

In return, the Kings will receive a 2028 Utah Jazz second-rounder and a 2030 Minnesota Timberwolves second-rounder out of the Thunder's deep asset cupboard.

The Kings initially acquired Clifford in the 2025 draft, trading a top-16-protected 2027 San Antonio Spurs first-round pick to the Thunder to move up to the No. 24 pick and grab Clifford. It was the first move of general manager Scott Perry's tenure.

But Clifford never caught on in Sacramento and has recently been buried in coach Doug Christie's rotation despite injuries ahead of him, leading both sides -- the Kings' and Clifford's -- to seek a new home for the 24-year-old.

The Thunder are in need on the wing after a rash of early-season injuries. Jalen Williams and Cason Wallace, both starters, are out for several months and perhaps the entire season. Wallace tore the labrum in his left shoulder and Williams fractured his left fibula and dislocated his left ankle in the same late October home game against the LA Clippers.

That led the Thunder to go searching for help, landing on Clifford, who is making only $3.2 million this season and $3.4 million next season. The Kings, in return, get a pair of draft assets and clear a roster spot as they search for any type of success in a 1-8 start to the season. The Thunder, despite the injuries, are 8-2.

stories.headline: What if Manchester United had hired Jurgen Klopp?
stories.summary: If Manchester United hired an all-time great like Jurgen Klopp, would they have won the Premier League? Let's find out!
stories.body:
Right around this time every year, you can start to feel it. The air gets a little crisper. The shadows get a little colder. The days get shorter. The tree colors start to pop. You start wearing sweaters. Pumpkins appear in places where they do and do not belong.

Everyone and everything starts to shift, just slightly, in preparation for what's about to happen. The cycles of nature can be fickle and unpredictable, so the date is never exactly the same, and some years come and go without anything at all. But most years, it does.

Our tiny little rituals prime us to anticipate the inevitable, oncoming shift: that moment when Manchester United fire their manager and convince themselves that the new guy is finally going to be the one who fixes everything.

Ruben Amorim lost his job last January. Erik ten Hag was fired two years ago, right before Halloween. Ole Gunnar Solskjaer got the boot just a couple of days before Thanksgiving. And Jose Mourinho was relieved of his duties a little over a week before Christmas.

Now that we've once again entered the season of sacking, Michael Carrick seems like he will inevitably become the latest victim.

Man United are in the relegation zone. If history is any indication, their comeback against AS Roma in the Champions League will end up being meaningless. Before Tuesday's win, Carrick appeared to be on the verge of tears at the end of every match.

This is the 14th season since Manchester United last won the Premier League. And whoever replaces Carrick will be the ninth coach to try to do something that no other United manager since has done: just, simply, meet the expectations at one of the richest sports teams on the planet for more than a single season in a row.

But given how many different coaches have now failed since Sir Alex Ferguson left the club, it makes you wonder: Could anyone have been successful at Manchester United?

What is a great manager worth?

Arsenal won the Premier League last season with 85 points.

If we lived in a world where there were no subs and everyone on the field contributed exactly evenly to their team's success, then all 11 Arsenal players would have contributed about 8 points (7.7, to be slightly more exact) of value last season.

Except, the alternative to each player isn't just zero points. If you removed Bukayo Saka from the lineup, you wouldn't have to play a man down. No, you'd get to put another player out there who would also contribute to winning to some degree.

So, let's look at the relegation-level cutoff. West Ham were relegated with 39 points. Using the same framework, we'd say that all of their players were worth a little over 3.5 points across the season. We could then say that the average Arsenal player provided 5 more points of value than a relegation-level player.

This, of course, isn't exactly how it works: Some players are better than others, some positions are more valuable than others, and almost nobody plays 100% of the minutes. Goalkeeper David Raya played 97.3% of the league minutes last season, and Declan Rice led all outfield Gunners with 90.5% of minutes played.

But it all still gives us a nice benchmark. The best players on the best teams in the world are probably worth around 7 points more than your average relegation-level player. The truly generational superstars? You could probably bump that number up to 10 points if you wanted to.

But what about the manager? Rather than litigating the whole "managers don't matter" conversation for the 1,000th time on this website, we're just going to go with the logic put forth by Liverpool's former director of research, Ian Graham, in his book, "How to Win the Premier League": "[About] the same value as a good player brings. This is in line with manager salaries -- the best managers are paid a similar wage to the best players."

Who, then, was the best manager that Manchester United could've hired at any point over the past 14 seasons?

Most soccer-watchers would agree that there are two potential answers: Pep Guardiola or Jurgen Klopp. And most analyses would agree.

A 2025 study from the Sloan Sports Analytics conference looked at team performances from 2017 through 2024 across Europe's Big Five top leagues. The study awarded or penalized the manager for how much a team's performance level exceeded or undershot expectations based on the talent of the roster. Klopp and Guardiola topped the list -- with a significant gap between themselves and the next tier of coaches.

Given the 114 guilty charges against Manchester City under Guardiola, though, I think we have to go with Klopp. While Guardiola's influence on how the sport is played is undeniable, we now have to look on his Man City tenure skeptically. We know how much they outperformed what we were told they spent, but it would be foolish to blindly accept those numbers and attribute the gap purely to the Guardiola effect.

With Klopp, though, we know that he turned two clubs that were not even the richest clubs in their own leagues into two of the best teams in the world. And we know that he maintained those levels -- at both clubs -- for many seasons in a row. On top of that, both Borussia Dortmund and now Liverpool seem to have gotten worse after he left each job.

The job of the manager, simply, is to make his team better than the talent his club can afford to acquire and then to keep that improvement going even as the roster turns over. At the highest level of the sport, Klopp was better at that than any of his peers.

Could the best manager in the world save Manchester United?

What, then, might've happened if Manchester United somehow managed to hire Jurgen Klopp back in 2013 instead of David Moyes?

There are, of course, all kinds of ripple effects we could tease out -- what it would've done to German soccer, where Liverpool would've ended up, how Mohamed Salah's career would've played out, and on and on.

But I just want to focus on what it would've meant for Manchester United. We know that Liverpool benefitted from hiring Jurgen Klopp. But we also know that Jurgen Klopp benefitted from working for a club that did things like convincing him to sign Mohamed Salah instead of Julian Brandt.

Liverpool's cutting-edge front office didn't turn the club into the best team in the world, and neither did Klopp. No, it was the combo of the two that did it.

We could say similarly about Borussia Dortmund. At the time, Dortmund were one of the leaders in both youth development and identifying young stars. This meant that Klopp got the ideal kinds of talent, energetic youngsters to play his high-pressing style: Robert Lewandowski, Mats Hummels, Marco Reus, and Ilkay Gündogan -- just to name a few.

What we know about Manchester United, broadly, is that the club is an abject disaster. In terms of doing things that increase their chances of winning games, they are pretty much as bad as it gets. Since 2013, United have finished at or higher in the table than their relative Premier League revenue ranking once -- and that was last season.

While we could employ some magical thinking and convince ourselves that the only problem here is that the club can't hire the right coach, that's obviously not true. If it were, it would mean that the club that keeps firing its coaches just so happens to be doing all of the other things right.

No, the failure to find a successful long-term coach is a symptom of all of the other issues that plague the club. They've so badly underperformed their resources for over a decade; we can confidently say there is something deeply wrong with the way Manchester United tries to build its soccer teams.

So, if Klopp were the Man United coach, he wouldn't have fixed all of those problems. No, he would've had to work within that dysfunctional environment. He would've, in other words, ended up with Brandt instead of Salah -- many times over.

But let's sketch out the absolute best-case scenario for this hypothetical. Let's say that United have continued to hire "relegation-quality" managers. And let's say that Klopp's value is equivalent not just to the best player on a title team but to a true, once-in-a-generation superstar.

Neither of those things is true -- United aren't constantly hiring genuinely bad coaches, and Klopp himself would tell you that he's not worth the same as Lionel Messi -- but stretching the effect out to the extreme helps make the point.

Plus, by applying a Messi-like effect every year, we're canceling out some of the other problems with this exercise: not addressing the Manchester City situation, not subtracting points from other teams, not accounting for the increased spending power from an increased performance level, and so on.

If Klopp could've added 10 points to every Manchester United season, here's how things would've changed:

On average, United would've ended up with 76 points per season instead of 66, and their average finishing position would've been 3.8 instead of 5.3.

So, of course: things would be better if Manchester United had employed the best manager of the modern era for the last decade-plus. In this scenario, they would've finished in the top four 10 times, rather than six. Perhaps there would've been a deep Champions League run at a club that reached three finals in four seasons from 2008 to 2011 and hasn't been beyond the quarterfinals since.

But even if we granted Manchester United 13 straight seasons of consistent, transformative, incomparable, once-in-a-generation managerial performance, the team would still find itself right where it sits today: with no Premier League titles since Sir Alex Ferguson left the club.

stories.headline: Gary Neville on Michael Carrick's Man United future: 'Ownership don't have a clue'
stories.summary: Gary Neville has slammed Manchester United's ownership, saying that they "don't have a clue what to do" about Michael Carrick's future at the club.
stories.body:
Gary Neville has slammed Manchester United's ownership, saying that they "don't have a clue what to do" about Michael Carrick's future at the club.

United will spend the international break in the relegation zone despite snatching a point in a topsy-turvy 4-4 draw with Aston Villa on Sunday thanks to stoppage-time goals from Joshua Zirkzee and Patrick Dorgu.

Having won one Premier League game all season, Carrick is under serious pressure -- a far cry from his position six months ago after guiding the club to third place as caretaker head coach.

"When the new manager comes in, everybody's happy for a couple of months and all of a sudden, six months later, it happens again," Neville told NBC.

"You can keep changing the manager and thinking that's going to be the answer. But this has been proven now over eight managers in 12 years, that's not the answer.

"Michael could leave, Michael might stay, we don't know, the ownership don't have a clue what to do."

United have not won the Premier League since Sir Alex Ferguson's final season, and have finished in the top four in fewer than half of seasons since then.

Fans protested against the Glazer family and Sir Jim Ratcliffe before and during Sunday's game, with some unveiling a banner reading: "We don't want a new stadium, we want new owners."

The club's chief executive, Omar Berrada, and director of football, Jason Wilcox, have also faced heavy criticism, with the latter even referenced by United defender Lisandro Martínez after the defeat to Atlético Madrid in October.

- Man United's poor starts have Premier League relegation looking more likely

- Man United in relegation zone, but Michael Carrick insists: I deserve to keep job

- Roy Keane likens Michael Carrick to 'politician' after chaotic Man United draw

"It's rinse and repeat," Neville said of United's strategy. "[Ruben] Amorim, [Erik] Ten Hag, Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, Carrick, José Mourinho, Louis van Gaal, David Moyes, Ralf Rangnick -- some of them are world class managers who have had success, there are a lot of promising young managers there, ex-players who know the club as well.

"None of it has worked because if you recruit badly, if you've got [a] poor performance department, poor recruitment department, you've not got leadership that is strong right through the spine of the football club you will fail.

"Every organisation in the world will fail if you've not got an aligned leadership from top to bottom -- your board and your ownership right the way through to the person who is stood on the pitch trying to play football.

"There are real issues within that football club, you've got people doing those jobs who have never done those jobs before in senior positions."

stories.headline: Pedro Martinez appeals for MLB resolution, reflects on effects of 1994 strike
stories.summary: Pedro Martinez appealed to both MLB players and owners to find a solution to their CBA talks, saying "get something done and don't lock out baseball for the fans."
stories.body:
Hall of Fame pitcher Pedro Martinez spoke out about the looming lockout hanging over Major League Baseball, saying a resolution must be found to protect the sport and fans.

"I feel for the fans, and I know when it's good, and it's good, baseball is good right now," Martinez said Saturday, according to the Boston Herald. "So stop the crap around and get something done and don't lock out baseball for the fans."

In Boston for the Pedro Martinez Foundation's 10th annual gala, Martinez said that "honestly speaking, I'm pissed" as he appealed to both players and owners to find a solution.

"Please, for the fans, both sides, figure it out, a good way to get it done, and do not lock out baseball," Martinez said.

The current collective bargaining agreement expires Dec. 1. MLB owners are trying to put a salary cap in place. Their latest offer, made Tuesday, would delay the implementation of the cap until 2028.

The players' union has remained steadfast against any talks of a salary cap during negotiations.

Martinez was hurt in multiple ways by a previous baseball stoppage early in his career. At the time of the 1994 strike, he was in his first season with the Montreal Expos, who had the best record in the majors at 74-40 and dreams of a World Series title when play was stopped. The cancellation of the rest of the 1994 season also kept Martinez a day away from arbitration eligibility.

"I hope the commissioner can see me and hear and the players' association hears what I have to say. I might be insignificant, but I lived it before. I experienced that before," Martinez said. "... I was one of the most punished players at that moment because I had talent, and I needed to wait until arbitration to make my money. So I hope they don't mess it up and they don't mistreat the fans."

"Back then, there was a need for other things to change, and they changed for the better. This time, there's no excuse," Martinez added in comparing the 1994 strike to today. "On both sides, not the PA, not the owners, not baseball. The fans do not deserve to be mistreated."

Martinez was a three-time Cy Young Award winner and eight-time All-Star who won the 2004 World Series with the Boston Red Sox and was inducted into the Hall of Fame in 2015.

stories.headline: Conor McGregor insists it has to be Max Holloway for final UFC fight
stories.summary: Conor McGregor has again insisted he only wants Max Holloway for his final UFC fight.
stories.body:
Conor McGregor has again insisted he only wants Max Holloway for his final UFC fight.

Back in July, Holloway (28-9) defeated McGregor (22-7) via TKO in just 69 seconds, after McGregor injured his right knee in the opening seconds of their welterweight bout in Las Vegas.

Speaking at the BKFC Glasgow post-fight news conference on Saturday, McGregor, 38, once again reiterated his desire to run it back with Holloway.

"It has to be Holloway," McGregor told reporters.

"Just do the f------ thing again. Just do the thing again. The guy didn't engage once. He's the one that called for the stoppage in the fight. He said 'ref, ref!'

"He's the one stopping the fight. Imagine I just said 'yay!' and jumped the fence. I won! He doesn't want to f------ fight.

"On the one leg, he wasn't coming near me. It's so shocking and so heartbreaking to me and I'm still f------ dealing with it. It has to be Holloway. Just f------ dust it off, re-do it."

On the rehab, McGregor stated he's looking for a return potentially before the summer next year and also hinted if Holloway isn't available he could look elsewhere for an opponent.

"I'm on my way back," McGregor said.

"What's it now November? Three months I'm off of surgery. I done this injury before and returned within nine months. So nine months is pre-summer. I just want to go again and again."

"Something might happen, I don't know. But a fighter that fights me, put some respect on my name. If you're not a world champion fighter, if you've not got world accolades to your name, don't utter my f------ name."

The fight against Holloway at UFC 329 was McGregor's first appearance since July 2021 and he has now suffered serious lower-body injuries in each of past two fights, including a fractured leg against Dustin Poirier in 2021.

stories.headline: LA Galaxy miss playoffs again as Real Salt Lake gets final berth
stories.summary: Sergi Solans and Zach Booth scored early and Real Salt Lake clinched a playoff spot while eliminating the LA Galaxy with a 2-1 Decision Day victory over the Galaxy on Saturday.
stories.body:
Sergi Solans and Zach Booth scored early and Real Salt Lake clinched a playoff spot while eliminating the LA Galaxy with a 2-1 Decision Day victory over the Galaxy on Saturday.

Real Salt Lake (13-15-6) snags the ninth and final postseason berth in the Western Conference and will travel to Seattle for a wild-card matchup with the Sounders. The winner will square off against the top-seeded Vancouver Whitecaps in the best-of-three first round.

The Galaxy (11-12-11) have missed the last two postseasons after winning the World Cup in 2024.

Solans and Booth scored three minutes apart to give Real Salt Lake a 2-0 lead in the 13th minute.

Solans used assists from Noel Caliskan and defender Philip Quinton in the 10th minute to score for the 14th time in his first season in the league. Nine of Caliskan's 11 career assists and all three of Quinton's have come this year.

Booth scored unassisted three minutes later for a 2-0 lead. It was the first goal for the 22-year-old rookie midfielder in his 18th appearance and seventh start.

The Galaxy cut it to 2-1 in the 40th minute thanks to an own goal by Real Salt Lake defender Luc de Fougerolles, making his seventh appearance in the league.

Rafael Cabral totaled one save for Real Salt Lake.

JT Marcinkowski saved six shots for Los Angeles.

The Galaxy beat Real Salt Lake 2-1 at home to close out April.

stories.headline: Wings' Paige Bueckers, Azzi Fudd talk relationship on pod
stories.summary: Azzi Fudd hosted Wings teammate Paige Bueckers on her podcast and the two discussed their relationship, Dallas' season and Fudd's recovery from knee surgery.
stories.body:
Dallas Wings teammates Azzi Fudd and Paige Bueckers, the past two WNBA No. 1 draft picks, spoke on Fudd's podcast Friday about a variety of topics, including a personal life update.

"We're not together anymore; it's been a while," Bueckers said on the "Fudd Around and Find Out" podcast. "[We] share that because everybody [was] like, 'Oh my gosh, they're teammates, how is this going to work?'"

Bueckers and Fudd, who were teammates in college at UConn, said they felt the need to address their relationship status in part because of allegations it factored into the Wings picking Fudd at No. 1 in April. Fudd was chosen over TCU guard Olivia Miles, who went on to be the Rookie of the Year for the Minnesota Lynx. Spain's Awa Fam (Seattle Storm) was taken third, followed by teammates from the 2026 champion UCLA Bruins: Lauren Betts (Washington Mystics), Gabriela Jaquez (Chicago Sky) and Kiki Rice (Toronto Tempo).

Fudd, Fam, Betts and Miles were all No. 1 at different points in ESPN's mock draft in the months before the April draft. Bueckers said her previous relationship with Fudd had no impact on Dallas' decision.

"We were not together before she got drafted," Bueckers said. "She was not drafted because she was my girlfriend. She was drafted because she deserved it. She's an amazing human, an amazing basketball player. And we're still friends, we're still cool.

"We played an entire season together; we're the utmost professionals."

Fudd averaged 13.1 points but was limited to just 30 games after an injury to her right knee led to season-ending arthroscopic surgery in August. She offered an update on her health.

"My offseason's been good," Fudd said. "Lots of rehab, lots of training, lots of on-court workouts, lots of traveling. It's been busy.

"I think there's a lot I can improve on. Especially the iso game; I feel like I'm not too comfortable with that yet. I know I'm capable of doing a little bit more. Watching someone like Paige who is able to create from anywhere ... that's great inspiration for me."

Bueckers averaged 20.9 points, 4.1 rebounds and 5.9 assists, and was named to the All-WNBA second team as Dallas reached the playoffs as the No. 7 seed.

The Wings were eliminated in the first round by the eventual champion Golden State Valkyries. Bueckers said she learned a lot from her first playoff experience and complimented Golden State.

"The Valkyries' defense, I can't explain to you how tough they are," Bueckers said. "They swarm, they send bodies, they trap you, they blitz you, they're so connected. I'm glad I got to have that experience against them to open my eyes to what the playoffs are like -- the physicality, the pressure, the environment.

"And I'm proud of our season. I hated losing; I sat and was pissed about it for like a week. I reached out to [Sue Bird] about it, what was her first playoff experience like. I didn't play as well as I wanted to. But it was my first experience, going against a really good opponent, and I was learning and growing through it all."

Fudd and Bueckers also addressed the Wings' move to the 19,000-seat American Airlines Center in downtown Dallas next season after playing at UT Arlington's College Park Center, which seats over 7,000, since the franchise relocated to Texas in 2016.

"UTA was a vibe; we had a ball, we did our thing there," Bueckers said. "But definitely excited to move into Dallas. New times."

While the change in venue will lead to more eyes on Wings games, the two players said they're hoping for less scrutiny of any on-court behavior.

Both said fans shouldn't read into interactions the two have with each other or their teammates as anything other than normal team behavior. They also said they don't stand for "hate of any kind" or "tearing people down to lift us up."

"We've seen a lot of negativity," Bueckers said. "We've had stuff sent to us, stuff sent to our family, our friends. There's been some crazy things said about us. We still support each other, we're still going to be great friends, we're still going to be great teammates. All the negative things can be put aside, and you don't need to overanalyze everything."

Fudd added with a chuckle, "Also, we don't need messages [from fans] on what the other person's doing. We've addressed everything we need to, and the rest will stay with us."

stories.headline: Kangaroos into World Cup final after thrashing Samoa
stories.summary: Australia have thrashed Samoa by 32 points to book a Rugby League World Cup final clash with New Zealand.
stories.body:
A backflipping Reece Walsh has helped put Australia within touching distance of their fourth-straight World Cup crown as the Kangaroos dismantled Samoa 44-12 in their semi-final.

In their most complete performance of the tournament to date, Kevin Walters' outfit put an ill-disciplined Samoan side to the sword, running in eight tries at Sydney's Allianz Stadium on Sunday night.

Led by fullback Walsh, who scored a hat-trick, the Kangaroos rarely looked troubled.

Australia will face New Zealand at Suncorp Stadium in Brisbane in next Sunday's final as they look to extend their stranglehold on the World Cup that stretches back to 2013.

"That's just Reece, he's always brings up something that you don't expect and the backflip was no different," said Walters.

"Tonight was a really good performance. I still think there's a bit more in us too, so that's exciting.

"Our middle forwards, I thought they stood up really well, they've been questioned and criticised by some people but not within our group."

As fluent as Australia were, Samoa were all at sea in one of their most underwhelming showings since their surprise run to the 2022 final.

With a side stacked with NRL talent and a groundswell of support from their diaspora community, Samoa have a realistic hope of breaking international rugby league's glass ceiling in the years to come.

But on Sunday they made nine errors and gave up 12 set restarts or penalties, while prop Spencer Leniu was sin-binned for dissent late in a disastrous first half.

Samoan coach Ben Gardiner claimed Australia benefited from "homeground calls".

"On the back of some of the penalties that were given, we just didn't react very well on the back of it," said Gardiner.

"Then it was one thing into another and then a try, so it made it really difficult to be able to fight back from that."

After a lively pre-game siva tau where they came face to face with the Kangaroos, Samoa were first on the board when Stephen Crichton kicked a fourth minute penalty.

But it was all one-way traffic from then on as Australia asserted their dominance, starting when Tom Dearden scythed through some feeble defence off a scrum play to put the home side on the board.

Jacob Preston pinballed his way over from close range before Tom Trbojevic, Walsh and Bradman Best all crossed to push the Kangaroos out to a 26-2 halftime lead.

Walsh - chosen ahead of James Tedesco for the starting No. 1 spot - celebrated his try with a backflip.

"He probably didn't need to do that but he did it for some sick kids," Walters explained.

But he was left red-faced soon after halftime when he leapt to claim a Samoa bomb, which Crichton scooped up to score.

The Brisbane fullback soon made amends by slaloming his way through the Samoan defence and palming off Brian To'o to add his second.

Izack Tago barged his way over as Samoa showed something of a fightback.

But again, Walsh was the man in the right place at the right time.

The fullback backed up a Cameron Munster break to add his third before having a hand in Australia's final try to winger Jack Bostock.

stories.headline: NFL Week 9: Big takeaways, questions and fantasy spin from Sunday's games
stories.summary: Our NFL Nation reporters react to all the action, answering the biggest questions coming out of each Sunday game. Here's what we learned from Week 9.
stories.body:
The Sunday slate for Week 9 of the 2026 NFL season kicked off in Madrid with the Bengals' offense erupting in a win over the Falcons. Cincinnati wide receiver Ja'Marr Chase finished with a season-high 155 yards and a touchdown on 10 receptions.

Back in the United States, the Lions defeated the Dolphins despite not scoring a touchdown in the first half. Rams edge rusher Myles Garrett returned from injury, finishing with three sacks in a win over the Commanders. And quarterback Bo Nix led the Broncos to their fifth fourth-quarter comeback of the season -- tied for the most in NFL history, per Elias Sports Bureau.

Our NFL Nation reporters react to all the action, answering lingering questions coming out of each game and detailing everything else you need to know. Fantasy football analysts Matt Bowen and Tristan Cockcroft also have fantasy takeaways from each matchup.

Let's get to it with the biggest lessons from Sunday.

Jump to:

NYJ-KC | DEN-CAR | LAR-WSH

DET-MIA | CIN-ATL

Catch up on Thursday's game:

JAX-BAL

Kansas City 35, N.Y. Jets 12
Catch up on the action: Box score | Recap

Chiefs
Should the Chiefs prioritize receiver or offensive line at the trade deadline?In a perfect scenario, the Chiefs would upgrade both positions. The more likely outcome is they acquire a receiver, as quarterback Patrick Mahomes hasn't completed a pass of 20-plus air yards since Week 4, when deep threat Tyquan Thornton suffered a dislocated ankle. Plus, it might be even more of a priority after Xavier Worthy's left hamstring injury in the fourth quarter Sunday. But Chiefs general manager Brett Veach should also be calling about an OT. Second-year left tackle Josh Simmons hasn't played this season because of a lower back injury. Right tackle Jaylon Moore also left Sunday's game with a right ankle injury.

Most surprising performance: Before this week, the Chiefs had only nine sacks, tied for the fewest in the league. But the Chiefs recorded more than half their previous season total on Sunday, sacking Jets quarterback Geno Smith five times. The last sack was significant one for defensive tackle Chris Jones, who now has the second most in sacks in franchise history (90.5). -- Nate Taylor

Next game: at Falcons (Sunday, 1 p.m. ET)

Jets
Should the Jets bench QB Geno Smith now and start positioning themselves for 2027? At some point, the Jets need to take a look at rookie Cade Klubnik, but this doesn't feel like the right time. Smith didn't play well Sunday, but he had been performing above expectations before then. Coach Aaron Glenn is on the hot seat and desperately needs wins to save his job, which is why he probably will stick with Smith until mathematical elimination. But make no mistake, this was ugly. Smith was sacked five times, squandered chances in scoring territory, and only 89 passing yards through three quarters. He was so frustrated that he spiked his helmet on the bench.

Key stat to know: After two sacks Sunday, rookie edge rusher David Bailey now has 7.5, the most by a first-round pick in his first eight games since Pro Football Hall of Famer Julius Peppers had nine in 2002. Bailey, drafted No. 2 overall, is New York's top foundational piece on defense. -- Rich Cimini

Next game: vs. Bills (Sunday, 1 p.m. ET)

Fantasy football takeaway: Chiefs RB Kenneth Walker III scored a season-high 36.3 points, which was his third game of 30-plus points this season. Walker, who had 143 total yards and three touchdowns on 22 touches, had two subpar games this season (SEA, DEN), but he remains the most consistent piece of the Chiefs' offense in fantasy scoring. -- Bowen

Denver 26, Carolina 21
Catch up on the action: Box score | Recap

Broncos
Will injuries in the Broncos' secondary finally catch up to them? Backup safety Devon Key's game-changing interception was just inches off the ground when he secured the ball. And that might be the margin for error for the Broncos this season. On a day when the team's starting safeties were gameday inactives, cornerback Riley Moss left Sunday's game in the second quarter with a concussion. The Broncos have already played three games this season without Pat Surtain II and four games without Talanoa Hufanga. Panthers QB Bryce Young threw three touchdowns, consistently targeting backups. The Broncos hope to have both starting safeties back after the bye, but an extended absence from Moss could hurt their nickel and dime packages.

What to make of the QB performance: Bo Nix continues to use the fourth quarter as his own personal football affirmation. After his red-zone interception midway through the second quarter gave the Panthers enough momentum to turn a 10-0 Broncos lead into Carolina's 14-13 lead in the third quarter, Nix again did fourth-quarter things. His 26-yard touchdown pass to Pat Bryant II came four minutes after he had closed out a 14-play, 81-yard touchdown drive. -- Jeff Legwold

Next game: vs. Raiders (Nov. 22, 4:25 p.m. ET)

Panthers
How much patience do Panthers deserve after DC switch? The unit, inherited by interim defensive coordinator Todd Wash this week, got off to a rough start Sunday. While a red-zone Corey Thornton interception and a Chau Smith-Wade pass breakup in the end zone mitigated some of the damage, the unit allowed a pair of big TD drives in the fourth quarter. Wash's debut saw Carolina surrender 312 net yards and three touchdowns (five scoring drives). The Panthers' makeshift starting cornerbacks, Thornton and Marco Wilson -- a pair of practice squad call-ups -- had five pass interference penalties (four accepted) that prolonged scoring drives.

Trend to watch: The Panthers haven't exceeded 21 points since their Week 6 win over the Eagles. Unsurprisingly, that's also the last time they won a game. The Panthers averaged 29.2 points per game in their first five games, starting 3-2. Since that early run, they've averaged 17.7 points per game and are now 3-5. -- Mike Kaye

Next game: at Saints (Sunday, 1 p.m. ET)

Fantasy football takeaway: WR Pat Bryant II's return from IR was a fruitful one: five targets for 15.6 fantasy points, including a 26-yard score. Bryant's upside and modest usage in this game could prove useful in deeper fantasy leagues and dynasties. He's available in 98.8% of ESPN leagues, and could be a worthy streamer for "byemaggedon" Week 11. -- Cockcroft

L.A. Rams 20, Washington 13
Catch up on the action: Box score | Recap

Rams
Will the Rams add a receiver before Tuesday's trade deadline? Not likely. Coach Sean McVay has said he doesn't expect to make a big move at the deadline, and the Rams don't have a lot of draft capital to work with. But until Davante Adams is back from his hamstring injury, the Rams are extremely thin at WR outside of Puka Nacua. On Sunday, Nacua had 14 catches for 150 yards and a touchdown on 19 targets. The other wide receivers combined for four catches for 36 yards. The Rams are above .500, but they've struggled to move the ball consistently this season. They were 3-for-14 on third-down against Washington.

Key stat to know: In his first game back from a knee injury, Rams edge rusher Myles Garrett had three sacks, his first three since being traded to Los Angeles in June. It was his first multisack game since Week 12 of last season, when he had three against the Raiders. -- Sarah Barshop

Next game: at Cardinals (Sunday, 4:05 p.m. ET)

Commanders
How does this loss impact Washington's trade deadline strategy? Washington might be mathematically alive for the NFC East title at 2-5-1, but the season clearly continues to head in the wrong direction. So it's fair to wonder how Sunday's loss impacts whether or not they make deals. Among those players who could be attractive to other teams: pass-rushing linebackers K'Lavon Chaisson and Dorance Armstrong, who are both on expiring deals. However, Washington might want to re-sign one or both for 2027. Also, the Commanders could still add a player -- like a high-ceiling receiver with more years on his contract.

What to make of the QB performance: Jayden Daniels completed 24 of 35 passes for 273 yards and a touchdown, but Washington's lone scoring drive after the first two series was set up by an interception deep in Rams' territory. The game highlighted the need for Washington to find him more help -- from the line to the run game. Daniels' big mistake was running loose with the ball, which led to a fumble and a Rams' field goal drive. -- John Keim

Next game: at Giants (Thursday, 8:15 p.m. ET)

Fantasy football takeaway: Rams RB Blake Corum's recent surge in usage has created a true backfield rotation in Los Angeles. Corum scored 11.8 points Sunday, rushing for 58 yards and a touchdown on 11 carries. He has now had 11 carries and a rushing score in three straight games, including double-digit points in five straight. Corum will move up into our RB2 rankings ahead of Week 10. -- Bowen

Detroit 19, Miami 9
Catch up on the action: Box score | Recap

Lions
Has the Lions defense gone from a weakness to a strength? Sure, the past two offenses they've faced -- Minnesota and Miami -- were the 26th and 31st scoring offenses entering Week 9, respectively, but the unit has now stacked four solid performances in a row. Through the first four weeks, Detroit's defense was second-to-last in points allowed (31.8). Since then -- in wins against the Cardinals, Packers, Vikings and Dolphins -- they've allowed just 17.0 per game. Given the Lions' normally high-scoring offense had struggled to score in each of the past two contests, the defensive turnaround couldn't have come at a better time.

Trend to watch: Sunday marked the second straight game in which the Lions failed to score a touchdown in the first half -- their first time doing so in consecutive games since October 2022. Part of the reason for that was quarterback Jared Goff being pressured on 40% of his dropbacks in the opening two quarters. -- ESPN staff

Next game: vs. Patriots (Sunday, 9:30 a.m. ET in Munich)

Dolphins
What does this performance say about the Dolphins' defense? The Lions entered Sunday's matchup leading the NFL in yards per game with 395.4, but they were held to just 120 at halftime. Miami's pass rush, which had just nine sacks in its previous seven games, sacked Goff three times and forced him to throw his second interception of the season. Ultimately, the Dolphins' defense kept them in this game while their offense floundered and has grown immensely over the course of the season -- specifically their young players. All five of Miami's interceptions in 2026 are by first- and second-year players.

Trend to watch: For the second straight week, the Dolphins averaged fewer than 4.0 yards per carry, as Detroit's ninth-ranked run defense lived up to its ranking. After five straight games of rushing for more than 100 yards, the Dolphins have now been held under 80 yards in consecutive games. Quarterback Malik Willis has also recorded single-digit rushing yards in back-to-back weeks. -- Marcel Louis-Jacques

Next game: at Colts (Sunday, 1 p.m. ET)

Fantasy football takeaway: Dolphins QB Malik Willis -- a popular streaming pick (season-high 15.1% start rate) -- scored an entirely forgettable 3.82 fantasy points. The groin issue that was brought to light during the game severely limited his mobility. Willis needs that facet of his game for him or his receivers to have any hope of streaming utility in future favorable matchups (Bills in Weeks 11 and 17; Bears in Week 14). -- Cockcroft

Cincinnati 34, Atlanta 17
Catch up on the action: Box score | Recap

Bengals
Has QB Joe Burrow established himself as the MVP? It's hard to argue against it, especially with how he has looked recently. One week after Burrow had six total touchdowns in an overtime win over the Titans, he put on an even more impressive performance against the Falcons, going 24-of-29 for 271 yards and three TDs. Burrow completed 16 of his first 18 passes and notably threw the ball much better than he did after tallying three interceptions last week. He's enhancing his case to finally break through and win an MVP after being a two-time finalist. And WR Ja'Marr Chase also played his part with a season-high 155 yards and a touchdown on 10 receptions.

Most surprising performance: Sunday was the day running back Chase Brown was looking for. He finally reeled off his first carry of 15 or more yards and put together a couple more big runs on Sunday. A dynamic rushing attack was the biggest thing the Bengals have been missing this season, and Brown's performance could be the catalyst to fixing that issue. He finished with 57 yards on nine carries for an average of 6.3 yards per carry. Samaje Perine added 43 yards on 11 carries. -- Ben Baby

Next game: vs. Steelers (Sunday, 8:20 p.m. ET)

Falcons
Will this loss change the Falcons' approach to the trade deadline? Probably not. There has been speculation the Falcons could move safety Jessie Bates III for draft picks. Bates will be a free agent after this season. The Falcons' 3-6 record does not look good, but the reality is they are still in the NFC South race and have the personnel to win the division if they can figure out a way to turn things around. Half of Atlanta's losses are with Cooper Rush starting at quarterback or in a driving rain. It doesn't seem like the Falcons are ready to pack it in for this season, especially since this franchise has not made the playoffs since 2017.

What to make of the QB performance: There was some good and mostly not good from Michael Penix Jr. The good? He showed the ability to make plays with his legs: a career-high 50 yards rushing. The bad? An inability to push the ball down the field with efficiency en route to just 5.2 yards per attempt. He finished 20-of-31 with a TD and a pick. -- Marc Raimondi

Next game: vs. Chiefs (Sunday, 1 p.m. ET)

Fantasy football takeaway: Falcons WR Drake London is no longer a surefire fantasy WR1. London faced a favorable matchup against the Bengals then saw only five targets and scored 11.8 fantasy points. Worse yet, his rest-of-November schedule is unfavorable: the Chiefs in Week 10, a bye week, at the Vikings in Week 11 and he also has matchups with the Browns (Week 14) and Buccaneers (Week 16). -- Cockcroft

stories.headline: 2026-27 NBA trade grades: Thunder acquire Nique Clifford from Kings
stories.summary: We're grading the biggest NBA trades of the season, including the deal that sent Nique Clifford to the Thunder.
stories.body:
The Oklahoma City Thunder and Sacramento Kings kicked off trade season Sunday, making a deal to send second-year wing Nique Clifford to the injury-ravaged Thunder for two future second-round picks. How does Clifford help replenish the Thunder's depleted depth alongside reigning MVP Shai Gilgeous-Alexander?

With three months to go until the Feb. 11 NBA trade deadline, expect more deals as the season goes on. I'm grading every trade and breaking down the ramifications for all teams and players involved.

To determine each grade, I'm looking at multiple factors, including the on-court impact and ages of involved players, the cost in terms of draft picks and future financial implications, and the context of the team's short- and long-term outlooks. How risky or certain is the move? And how much does it help or hurt the team's chance to win the championship this season or beyond?

Let's get into the latest moves:

Quick links:

Latest buzz | Trade machine

Depth charts

Nov. 8: Kings trade G Clifford to Thunder

Sacramento Kings get: 2028 second-round pick (via Utah), 2030 second-round pick (via Minnesota)

Oklahoma City Thunder get: G Nique Clifford

Grade for Kings: C-

On the night of the 2025 draft, the Kings traded a future top-16-protected pick from the San Antonio Spurs to Oklahoma City for the No. 24 pick, which they used on Clifford. Less than 18 months later, they're sending Clifford back to the Thunder.

That would be a strange use of resources on its own -- two second-round picks is a less valuable package than a protected first -- but the Kings' choices look even stranger when considering what happened in the meantime: Clifford was perfectly capable as a rookie before being inexplicably buried on Sacramento's bench to start his sophomore season.

Last season, Clifford averaged 8.6 points, 3.8 rebounds and 2.4 assists in 25.1 minutes per game, and he posted the best on/off swing in Sacramento's rotation. But this season, he's down to 1.6 points in 6.3 minutes per contest.

To be fair, Clifford is already 24 years old and appears to have a limited NBA ceiling. If the Kings truly concluded that he didn't fit on their roster anymore, then at least they got some draft capital back for him.

But it's unclear why they would have come to that conclusion, given his play in 1,932 NBA minutes so far.

Grade for Thunder: B

The Thunder entered the weekend with 21 future second-round picks, which is far more than they'd ever actually have room to use. So they cashed in two of them for an immediate upgrade on the wing, where injuries have stressed even the Thunder's enviable depth.

Clifford might not end up playing any role for Oklahoma City come playoff time, but the team simply needs bodies in the meantime, and Clifford should be useful on both ends in a regular-season capacity. And who knows? Place him in the Thunder's excellent development system and he might blow past any theoretical ceiling while offering inexpensive production for the next few years.

stories.headline: Elias Lindholm scores 1st of Boston's 3 goals in 1st period, carrying Bruins past Panthers, 4-1
stories.summary: — Elias Lindholm, Mikey Eyssimont and Morgan Geekie each scored a goal in an opening period that started out testy, carrying the Boston Bruins past the Florida Panthers 4-1 on Sunday.
stories.body:
BOSTON -- — Elias Lindholm, Mikey Eyssimont and Morgan Geekie each scored a goal in an opening period that started out testy, carrying the Boston Bruins past the Florida Panthers 4-1 on Sunday.


Jeremy Swayman made 40 saves, 17 coming in the first period, for the Bruins, who improved to 7-0-0 at home by winning their fourth straight game a day after placing young star James Hagens on injured reserve.


JJ Peterka added a goal for Boston, which owns a plus-21 goal differential at TD Garden. David Pastrnak and Pavel Zacha each added two assists.


Carter Verhaeghe scored a power-play goal for the Panthers, and Jacob Markstrom stopped 32 shots. Florida has lost three of four games.


Boston’s 6-foot-7 defenseman Nikita Zadorov dropped the gloves against 6-foot-1 forward Brady Tkachuk at the opening faceoff, setting the stage for 126 total penalty minutes.


Just over six minutes later, Florida’s Garnet Hathaway squared off against forward Mark Kastelic.


The Panthers swept the three games against Boston last season, winning each by one goal.


Following a lengthy review, Lindholm was credited with a goal that made it 1-0 just 4:50 into the game after his wrister broke off Markstrom and trickled behind him, nearing the goal line as he attempted to pull it back with his glove.


Eyssimont poked a loose puck into the net following his wraparound shot, making it 2-0 less than two minutes later.


Geekie then scored for the fourth straight game, one-timing a shot for a power-play goal at 15:59 with the Bruins on a two-man advantage.


Verhaeghe’s one-timer cut it to 3-1.


The Bruins, who entered with the NHL’s second-best goal differential behind Carolina, were off since rolling to a 6-2 victory at Pittsburgh on Thursday.

stories.headline: Bayern Munich's Manuel Neuer set for spell on sidelines with foot injury
stories.summary: Bayern Munich goalkeeper Manuel Neuer sustained a partial ligament tear in his right foot and will be out of action for "the time being," the club said in a statement on Sunday.
stories.body:
Bayern Munich goalkeeper Manuel Neuer sustained a partial ligament tear in his right foot and will be out of action for "the time being," the club said in a statement on Sunday.

Neuer had to go off with the injury shortly before halftime in Bayern's 2-1 Bundesliga win at Mainz on Saturday.

Bayern's statement did not give a specific length of layoff for the German goalkeeper, only stating it would be 'for the time being'.

"Manuel Neuer will be out of action for FC Bayern for the time being," the club said.

"The captain sustained a partial tendor tear in his right foot during the German record champions' 2-1 win against 1.FSV Mainz 05 on Saturday, as confirmed by an examination by the FC Bayern medical unit.

"Neuer was substitued shortly before half-time at Mainz."

Replacement goalkeeper Jonas Urbig filled in, as he has often done for the veteran Neuer this season. Urbig is viewed as Neuer's long-term successor at the club and the injury presents a chance to demonstrate he can eventually take the role.

The injury is another blow to Bayern's season following Vincent Kompany's battles with issues that saw him collapse at training. He was hospitalised and treated for meningeal irritation, which is an inflammation of the tissue around the brain or spinal cord.

Neuer has only made five league appearances this season, while the 23-year-old Urbig has also made five, including his substitute appearance Saturday.

It was a bittersweet moment for Neuer as he also became Bayern's oldest Bundesliga player at 40 years and 225 days old in the game.

stories.headline: Man United in relegation zone, but Michael Carrick insists: I deserve to keep job
stories.summary: Michael Carrick insisted there's enough evidence that he should keep his job despite Manchester United sitting in the Premier League relegation zone.
stories.body:
Michael Carrick insisted there's enough evidence that he should keep his job despite Manchester United sitting in the Premier League relegation zone.

United staged a dramatic late fightback to draw 4-4 with Aston Villa on Sunday. But with just one league win all season, Carrick's team are in the bottom three ahead of the international break.

Villa were twice up by two at Old Trafford -- 2-0 and 4-2 -- before they were stunned by two goals in stoppage time from Joshua Zirkzee and Patrick Dorgu.

The rousing finale is unlikely to quiet questions about Carrick's position. However, the 45-year-old said he believes there are enough positives to suggest that he should be in charge when United next play against Liverpool at Anfield on Nov. 22.

"Yeah, 100%, yeah," Carrick said at the postmatch news conference. "I think there's more than enough. Goals change games and you've got to deal with it, and it's part of something we have to improve on drastically, but there's more than enough. We're just making it too difficult for ourselves at the moment in certain times.

"I'm quite clear with what direction the club needs to go in, and it's got to win games."

Before arriving for his postmatch news conference, Carrick was involved in an awkward exchange during a TV interview with Sky Sports.

- 'Like a politician': Keane calls for more from Carrick after United draw

- What if Manchester United had hired Jurgen Klopp?

- Poor starts have Man United facing relegation battle

Asked whether there would be conversations with the club's hierarchy in the coming days, Carrick said: "Is there?"

When it was suggested that fans would "assume so," Carrick replied: "Would you?

"We haven't won enough games, but I expect to move forward and keep working on what we've been working on, tighten up on a few mistakes, and win football matches."

Carrick was also asked by Sky Sports whether he would consider quitting. The former England midfielder said: "That's not going to happen."

stories.headline: Witness: Clase 'inside' pitch info dried up amid Mizuhara case fallout
stories.summary: A witness said that the inside info he used to bet on Clase pitches dried up due to increased scrutiny from the scandal involving Shohei Ohtani's interpreter.
stories.body:
NEW YORK -- A government witness testified Friday in the federal trial of Cleveland Guardians pitchers Emmanuel Clase and Luis Ortiz that the inside information he used to bet regularly on Clase pitches in 2023 dried up the next season due to increased scrutiny from the gambling scandal involving Shohei Ohtani's interpreter at the time.

Luis de Aza Baez said he placed dozens of bets and won thousands of dollars by wagering on the velocity of select Clase pitches during the 2023 season, "because I had inside information." Clase is accused of conspiring with bettors to rig 18 pitches over three seasons.

De Aza Baez said that when he asked for more information on Clase pitches in 2024, he was told that because of "what was going on with Ohtani, there was no more information like that."

Ohtani, the Los Angeles Dodgers' superstar, came under scrutiny in March 2024 after ESPN reported that millions of dollars had been sent from his bank account to an illegal bookmaking operation. His longtime interpreter, Ippei Mizuhara, later pleaded guilty to stealing nearly $17 million from Ohtani to pay off gambling debts and is currently in prison. Ohtani was cleared of any wrongdoing.

De Aza Baez, who worked as an Uber driver, told prosecutors that he began receiving information about the pitches from Enoc Pena, an associate of Clase's, in 2023. De Aza Baez said the tips often came through a group chat titled "Uber Inc." that Pena started and included other men who have been referenced in the case and also worked for the ride-share company in Massachusetts at the time.

Prosecutors showed a screenshot of a text message Clase allegedly sent to Pena on Sept. 30, 2023, when the Guardians were scheduled to play the Detroit Tigers, that talked about "killing the first two chickens." De Aza Baez said the message was instructions to bet on a Clase pitch to the third batter of an inning, but only if Clase had retired the first two batters. Clase did not appear in the game.

Clase's defense has argued that mentions of roosters and chickens in such communications often were referencing cockfighting, a legal activity in the Dominican Republic, where Clase and others in the case are from.

De Aza Baez said he became friends with Pena as well as Robinson Vásquez Germosen and Luis Arismendy Paca Méndez, who are co-defendants in the case, while they were all living in Nantucket, Massachusetts. Paca Méndez, who has pleaded not guilty, is not participating in the trial after being extradited from the Dominican Republic to the U.S. on Oct. 19.

De Aza Baez said he met Clase when Vásquez and Pena brought the pitcher to his house for a birthday party on April 28, 2023, in Winthrop, Massachusetts, where De Aza Baez had moved. He met Clase again a few days later at a relative's house. Prosecutors showed a video of the gathering, with Clase playing dominoes on a table featuring a Boston Red Sox logo. The Guardians were in town for a series against the Red Sox.

De Aza Baez said he never received any information directly from Clase, only from Pena. De Aza Baez said he did not have an agreement with Pena but gave him money because he "almost always" won using the information to bet on Clase's pitches. De Aza Baez acknowledged opening a DraftKings betting account under his wife's name to increase the amount he could wager and win on his Clase bets. De Aza Baez also said he included the Clase pitch bets in parlays to maximize payouts.

De Aza Baez acknowledged that he had agreed with the government to forfeit $69,000 from his winning bets on Clase and would "tell the truth" in exchange for prosecutors dropping a wire fraud charge related to the case.

Clase, Ortiz and Vásquez have pleaded not guilty to conspiracy charges of wire and honest services fraud, sports bribery and money laundering.

"Our defense is the same today as it was in opening: This is a case about big talk and small bets," Vásquez's attorney Todd Spodek told ESPN after Friday's hearing. "We're confident leaving that judgment to the jury."

The trial will continue next Thursday in Brooklyn.
